## Claude synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful with Caveats

Camp, Anglum, Koedel, Lee, and Nguyen give the field the most current causal evidence on whether Missouri's four-day school week (4DSW) does what its adopters say it does: using statewide teacher-level administrative data from 2008–09 through 2023–24, a Gardner et al. two-stage difference-in-differences with not-yet-treated adopters as the only controls, and the full post-COVID wave that took Missouri from 33 to 178 four-day districts, they find that adoption did not detectably reduce teacher exits (−0.006, SE 0.007, on a pre-adoption base of 0.126; Table 2), did not raise the new-hire share of the workforce (0.001, SE 0.006; Table 3), and did shift the origin of new hires toward teachers from other Missouri districts (+0.011, SE 0.003) and away from teachers new to Missouri teaching (−0.010, SE 0.004). The retention null is the paper's load-bearing result and it holds up: flat pre-trends, stability across the saturation specification and the 151 spillover-exclusion thresholds, and a bias direction (poaching from not-yet-treated neighbors would make adoption look *good* for retention) that runs against a hidden benefit. It should replace or sit beside Thompson (2025) as the reference citation for Missouri, and it moves the multi-state literature — positive in Texas and modestly Arkansas, null in Colorado and Missouri/Oklahoma, negative in Oregon — further toward "little or no retention effect." The caveats attach to how the paper talks about that null and to its two secondary claims. "No evidence of practically meaningful 4DSW impacts" is a point-estimate sentence; the 95% interval reaches about 2 fewer exits per 100 teachers, roughly 16% of baseline turnover, which is not a tight zero and is larger than the composition shift the paper then interprets as "nontrivial." The abstract's "composition of new hires shifts toward more experienced teachers" restates an origin measure (from another Missouri district vs. new to Missouri teaching) as an experience measure the paper does not directly find (p. 21 reports insignificant experience effects, in an appendix not available to this review), and the paper's own Figure 5 shows the from-another-district estimate drifting toward zero and its band covering zero once controls within roughly the median mover distance (41 km) are excluded — a pattern the text reads permissively. The "perception versus reality" frame that the introduction calls the most interesting takeaway compares interviewees' claims about applicant volume and satisfaction, which the data never measure, with exit and hire-share outcomes, and it does not confront the fact that the one robust positive result is consistent with what superintendents describe. Add a cluster of production-level inconsistencies (an early/late adopter definition stated two ways; a Table 6 note describing district-level models as teacher-level; treatment timing indexed t+1 in Equations 1–2 and t in Equation 4; exit outcomes plotted under a "retention" axis label; 554 vs. 559 districts), no data availability, code, or software statement, and a supplement that carries every alternative-estimator, control-group, covariate, and pre-COVID robustness check, and the right posture is: rely on the retention null and quote its interval; cite the composition shift as a reallocation of experienced in-state movers with the spillover caveat attached; and treat the "information problem" framing as the authors' interpretation rather than a demonstrated finding.

#### Key Strengths

- The design is well chosen for the setting and executed with current tools. Adopters differ sharply from never-adopters (Table 1, Panel A: average salary \$44,718 vs. \$54,909; rural share 46.1% vs. 10.9%), so the paper compares adopters only with not-yet-treated adopters and uses the Gardner et al. (2024) two-stage estimator to block forbidden comparisons; it clusters at the district (about 178 clusters), omits covariates on principled grounds, and reports pre-adoption means so every estimate can be scaled.
- The retention null is the most robust object in the paper. It is stable across Table 2, the saturation model (−0.007, Table 5), the event study (Figure 2), and the spillover-exclusion path (Figure 4), it is not the product of an outcome definition a replicator could easily overturn, and the two plausible SUTVA violations (adopters recruit from neighbors; adoption follows a turnover spike) both bias *toward* finding a benefit, so a null survives them.
- The robustness program is unusually complete for the question: a Butts (2024) spatial-spillover test over every integer distance from 0 to 150 km, commuting-zone saturation interactions, a re-estimation using only the 22 interviewed districts as treated, a pre-COVID subsample, alternative control groups with covariate pre-trend plots, and three alternative staggered-DiD estimators — although all but the spillover and saturation exhibits live in a supplement this review could not open.
- The paper tests a practitioner belief against administrative data in the same state and sample. The 36 interviews (20 superintendents, 4 principals, 12 teachers in 22 districts) are thinly documented, but pairing them with the quantitative estimates, and then re-running the models on the interviewed districts alone, is a model for evaluating policies whose case rests on what adopters perceive.
- Prose and tables agree on every headline number. "0.6 fewer exits per 100," "1.3 fewer STEM exits," and "on the order of 1 FTE per 100" all match Tables 2 and 3; Table 2's exit components sum to any-turnover in every column; and the authors apply the von Hippel–Schuetze "no, but" caution to their own STEM coefficient.

#### Key Concerns

- The null is framed by its point estimate, not its interval. The introduction's "no evidence of practically meaningful 4DSW impacts" (p. 2) and the results' "very small" (p. 11) describe −0.006; the data are consistent with anything from a 2-point reduction (about 16% of baseline) to a small increase, and for STEM teachers with reductions of up to a quarter of baseline. The claim that vacancy confounding is "largely ruled out" by the retention null (p. 12) rests on the same point-estimate reasoning.
- The composition shift is less settled than the abstract implies. Figure 5 shows the from-another-district estimate moving toward zero as spillover-exposed controls are excluded, with the band including zero from roughly 50 km on — near the 41-km median move distance — and the paper's stated test (do the bands still cover the d = 0 estimate?) cannot distinguish "no bias" from "estimate no longer distinguishable from zero." The abstract's "more experienced teachers" is inferred from origin, not measured; the direct experience test is described as insignificant and underpowered (p. 21).
- The special-education "boost" featured in the introduction (p. 2) is one 10%-significant cell (0.022, SE 0.012) in a 12-estimate table, falls to 0.015 (SE 0.014) in the saturation specification (Table 6), and is exactly the kind of "no, but" subgroup result the authors warn against three pages earlier; only its from-another-district component (0.029, SE 0.006) is robust.
- The perception-vs-reality conclusion outruns the design. Interviewees' concrete evidence was applicant volume, which the paper cannot observe (note 10); the qualitative section gives no counts behind "overwhelmingly" or "a handful of dissenters"; and the paper's own significant result — more experienced in-state movers — is consistent with the recruitment advantage superintendents describe. Two cited predecessors (Thompson 2025; Camp 2024) report that nearby four-day adoption harms retention in five-day neighbors, which is not engaged; the spillover section tests bias in the treatment effect, not harm to non-adopters, and never reports the spillover coefficient itself.
- The reader must resolve several inconsistencies and take much on trust. Text (p. 6) and Table 1 note (p. 8) define the early/late split differently; Table 6's note calls district-level models "teacher-level"; Equations 1–2 index treatment at t+1 while Equation 4 uses t and the fixed-effect symbols change between them; Figures 2 and 4 plot exits under a "Change in Teacher Retention" axis; Table 1 sums to 554 districts against 559 in the text; Table 3, column 3's components sum to 0.115 against a reported 0.117; p. 21 speaks of excluding "nonrural, never-treated" districts when pp. 6 and 19 say the controls are not-yet-treated only. There is no data availability statement, access pathway, code, or software statement, the non-confidential adoption-year list is not released, and Appendices A–E carry the alternative estimators, covariates, control groups, interview-district test, pre-COVID sample, and salary/experience trends.

#### What to Rely On

- Adopting the four-day week in Missouri did not produce a detectable reduction in teacher turnover, overall or for high-need, STEM, or special-education teachers. Quote it as −0.006 (SE 0.007) on a pre-adoption mean of 0.126 (Table 2, Panel A row 1, col. 1) with flat pre-trends (Figure 2), and read it as "reductions larger than about 2 exits per 100 are unlikely," not as "the effect is zero."
- Adopting districts did not expand their teacher workforce, as measured by the new-hire share of FTE (0.001, SE 0.006; Table 3, Panel A row 1, col. 1), confirmed by the event study in Figure 3.
- The retention null does not depend on how saturated the local market already was at adoption: the 4DSW × prevalence interaction is 0.010 (SE 0.050) for any turnover (Table 5), and the main coefficients barely move when it is added. This extends Thompson (2025)'s Missouri null through the post-2019 wave.
- Adopters draw relatively more new hires from other Missouri districts and fewer who are new to Missouri teaching (Table 3, Panel A rows 2–3, col. 1: +0.011 and −0.010; about +23% and −13% of their pre-adoption means). Cite this as a reallocation of experienced in-state movers, with the Figure 5 caveat attached.
- The 4DSW did not detectably reduce out-of-field teaching in high-need fields (Table 4), though the estimates are imprecise and no baseline is reported.
- Educators in adopting districts overwhelmingly believe the policy helps recruitment and retention, and frame it as a substitute for salary (pp. 4–5). This is consistent with prior interview work in Arkansas and with the RAND multi-state study; cite it as confirmation, not discovery.
- Missouri's adopters are small, rural, lower-paying districts with higher baseline turnover (Table 1); the 178 districts contain 13% of the state's teachers and 12% of its students (Figure 1).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- "No practically meaningful impact on retention" — the 95% interval runs to about −0.020, roughly 16% of baseline turnover and larger than the composition shift the paper interprets; the paper never states the range. For STEM teachers the interval admits reductions of about a quarter of baseline.
- "The composition of new hires shifts toward more experienced teachers" (abstract) — the measured variable is origin, not experience; the paper reports the direct experience test as insignificant (p. 21, appendix not available); and under the paper's own spillover exclusion the from-another-district estimate is not distinguishable from zero beyond about 50 km (Figure 5).
- "A boost in special education recruitment" (introduction) — one marginal cell in a 12-estimate table that loses significance in Table 6; only the from-another-district SPED component is robust.
- "No indication that spillover effects are causing bias" — the test asks whether the d = 0 estimate stays inside the bands, which it does even when the bands also include zero. For retention this is reassuring because the estimate is flat across d; for recruitment it is uninformative, and the paper does not report the spillover coefficient or test whether non-adopting neighbors are harmed, which two cited predecessors found.
- "Strong evidence of parallel pre-trends ... with small confidence intervals" — pre-period coefficients in two-stage/imputation event studies are computed from the same untreated observations used to fit the first stage, so their narrow bands (visibly narrower than post-period bands in Figures 2–3) are weaker evidence than they look; the event-study window, binning, and reference periods are unstated, and both −6 and −1 are pinned at zero.
- "The scope for saturation to influence the treatment effect is very small" — a point-estimate claim; scaled by the 0.095 SD, the interaction SE of 0.050 permits moderation of about ±1 point per SD, the same size as the effects at issue.
- "A substantial gap between perception and reality" / "a significant information problem" — the perceptions most concretely cited (applicant volume) are unmeasured, the interview sample is neither counted nor selected transparently, and the one robust positive result is consistent with what interviewees describe. Read as "perceived large gains are not visible in exit or hire-share data."
- The literature summary quoted from this paper — seven of the eight retention studies it cites are working papers; Thompson (2025) is characterized as "null in each state individually" (verify against its heterogeneity tables); the −0.02 to −0.09 SD achievement range excludes the cited Nowak et al. metropolitan estimate and omits Thompson's Oregon *Journal of Public Economics* study; Nowak et al. studied a suburban Denver-area district, not "Denver"; and the *EEPA* scoping review by Grant et al. is not cited.
- Any number a reader must reconstruct from the connective tissue: the early/late adopter cutoff (follow the text's "adopted by 2020–21 = early," which matches N = 106), the 554/559 district count, the Table 3 column 3 sum, the Table 4 observation counts (2,651–2,658 vs. 2,673), and the treatment-timing convention across Equations 1–4.
- Every "substantively similar" robustness claim — alternative estimators (A.3–A.5), covariates (A.2), district aggregation (A.1), alternative control groups and salary/experience trends (C), the interview-district test (D), and the pre-COVID sample (E) — is asserted in prose and lives in a supplement this review could not examine; none can be verified from the article, and none can be reproduced without DESE access, the authors' adoption-year file, and code the paper does not provide.

## Codex synthesis

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This paper provides useful Missouri evidence against assuming that a four-day school week will reliably solve teacher staffing problems. Its staggered-adoption difference-in-differences analysis finds no statistically detectable average change in teacher turnover or the overall new-hire share, but finds a shift toward hires from other Missouri districts and away from hires new to teaching in Missouri (p. 12, Table 2; p. 14, Table 3). The contribution extends earlier Missouri retention research with newer observations, recruitment composition, and educator interviews; it is a meaningful empirical extension rather than a field-changing result (p. 3). My assessment is useful with caveats: the comparison strategy is credible under its identifying assumptions, but the retention estimates do not rule out worthwhile benefits, and hiring shares do not directly measure applicant supply, recruitment ease, or workforce size. Favorable educator accounts can therefore coexist with the administrative findings. The paper deserves selective citation for its measured outcomes, primarily in settings resembling Missouri adopters, while its stronger claims about negligible benefits, mistaken perceptions, and inconsequential market saturation need qualification. Documentation gaps and unavailable supplements limit independent verification without demonstrating that the published estimates are wrong.

#### Key Strengths

- A substantively motivated comparison and suitable staggered-adoption estimator: the preferred design compares adopters with not-yet-treated districts and avoids using already-treated observations to estimate the counterfactual fixed effects; district clustering matches policy assignment. My judgment is that these choices strengthen the design, although they do not establish parallel untreated trends (pp. 6, 9–10).
- Administrative records distinguish district exits and hiring origins, while the main tables report uncertainty and baseline means. The recruitment decomposition reveals changes concealed by the aggregate hiring result (p. 12, Table 2; p. 14, Table 3).
- Directly inspectable event studies and spatial sensitivity analyses make the empirical argument assessable. The displayed pre-adoption patterns are reassuring, and the retention results are broadly stable across the spatial specifications; these are supporting diagnostics rather than proof of identification (p. 13, Figure 2; p. 15, Figure 3; p. 17, Figure 4).
- The literature discussion acknowledges the closest Missouri antecedent and conflicting findings elsewhere, while the interviews explain the staffing rationale for adoption and include dissenting accounts. This combination gives readers useful context for an incremental, policy-relevant contribution (pp. 3–5, 22).

#### Key Concerns

- A nonsignificant retention estimate does not establish negligible effects. The all-subject turnover estimate is −0.006 (SE 0.007); my normal-approximation 95% interval, calculated from the rounded published values, is −1.97 to +0.77 percentage points. A potentially worthwhile reduction remains compatible with the estimate (p. 12, Table 2, panel A, row 1, all-subjects column).
- Recruitment is measured as new-hire FTE divided by total relevant FTE, not applications, hiring effort, vacancy duration, or a direct workforce-size effect (p. 14, Table 3 note; pp. 10–12; pp. 23–24, note 10). The discussion allows that districts are 'not trying to hire more teachers' (p. 12), whereas the conclusion says adoption 'does not result in districts expanding their teacher workforce' (p. 22). My judgment is that the latter inference is stronger than the displayed hiring-share evidence and cannot establish that interviewees' perceived benefits are mistaken.
- Causal interpretation remains conditional on parallel untreated trends and uncontaminated comparisons. Pretrends cannot exclude adoption-time staffing shocks or differential pandemic effects. Wider spatial exclusions move hiring-composition estimates toward zero and increase uncertainty, while saturation is measured at adoption rather than as neighbors subsequently adopt; these exercises do not rule out all competitive mechanisms (pp. 9–10, 19, 21; p. 18, Figure 5; p. 20, Tables 5–6).
- Independent reproduction is limited by missing code and data-access instructions in the supplied article, incomplete construction rules, and unavailable online appendices (pp. 5–6, 10–11, 19–24). A verified notation discrepancy compounds the problem: Equation 1 prints '4DSW_{jt+1}' (p. 6), but Equation 4 prints '4DSW_{jt}' (p. 10). This requires clarification; it is not evidence of a coding error. Exhibit labels also require care: Figure 3's caption identifies 'new teacher FTE shares' but its axis says 'Change in Teacher Retention' (p. 15).

  > **Correction (2026-09-25).** This review states that Figure 3's vertical axis reads "Change in Teacher Retention." On the rendered page (p. 15) it reads "Change in Teacher Recruitment." The parallel observation about Figure 2 (p. 13), whose axis does read "Change in Teacher Retention" over exit outcomes, is correct. Found during comparison with the independent Claude review.

- The evidence is bounded by the adopting-district population and the outcomes studied. Adopters differ substantially from never-adopters (p. 8, Table 1), and this study does not estimate student achievement, family consequences, or a complete policy cost-benefit balance. The paper itself reports mixed retention evidence across states and qualifies the achievement literature by implementation, limiting a general recommendation to reverse adoption (pp. 3–4, 22–23, notes 3–4).

#### What to Rely On

- No statistically detectable average turnover change among the studied Missouri adopters under the difference-in-differences assumptions: this is evidence against treating retention gains as established, not evidence of an exactly zero or necessarily negligible effect (p. 12, Table 2; p. 13, Figure 2).
- A hiring-origin shift in the preferred specification: hires from other Missouri districts increase by 1.1 percentage points and hires new to teaching in Missouri decrease by 1.0 percentage point, each measured against total district teacher FTE, not against new hires alone (p. 14, Table 3, panel A, rows 2–3 and note).
- No statistically detectable change in the overall new-hire FTE share or the displayed out-of-field teaching rates: these conclusions concern the measured shares, not every dimension of staffing success (p. 14, Table 3; p. 16, Table 4).
- Participating educators commonly describe staffing and job-amenity benefits as reasons to favor the calendar: the interviews document those accounts, with an explicit warning that the interviewed districts are not representative (pp. 4–5).

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Claims that the policy has no meaningful retention benefit, cannot make hiring easier, or disproves favorable educator perceptions: the retention interval remains consequential, the hiring outcomes omit applicant supply and recruitment effort, and the interviews address partly different outcomes (p. 12, Table 2; p. 14, Table 3; pp. 4–5, 10–12, 22; pp. 23–24, note 10).
- Claims of better teacher effectiveness or a larger statewide teacher supply: movement from another Missouri district establishes hiring origin, not effectiveness or a statewide net gain; 'new to teaching in Missouri' also need not mean new to teaching everywhere (p. 14, Table 3; p. 10).
- A dependable special-education recruitment gain: the overall new-hire-share estimate is 0.022 (SE 0.012), marked only marginally significant, amid multiple outcome and subgroup comparisons; my judgment is that it is suggestive rather than a settled subgroup result (p. 14, Table 3, panel A, row 1, SPED column).
- Assertions that spillovers or saturation do not matter: retention estimates are comparatively stable, but the hiring-composition results weaken under wider spatial exclusions, and imprecise adoption-time interactions cannot exclude dynamic erosion of a recruitment advantage (pp. 17–18, Figures 4–5; p. 19; p. 20, Tables 5–6).
- Claims of fully verified robustness or a general policy verdict: alternative-estimator, salary, comparison-group, interview-sample, and pre-pandemic checks are described but their supplemental exhibits are unavailable; broader policy conclusions also depend on outcomes and implementation differences beyond this evaluation (pp. 10–11, 19–23).

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution reviews: the turnover coefficient and SE are −0.006 and 0.007; independently recalculated normal-approximation 95% interval is −1.97 to +0.77 percentage points, not an interval printed by the authors (p. 12, Table 2, panel A, row 1).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution/writing reviews: hiring-origin coefficients are 0.011 and −0.010, and the denominator is total district teacher FTE; these are not shares of new hires or a direct workforce-size estimate (p. 14, Table 3, panel A, rows 2–3 and note).
- CONFIRMED — Methods review: the special-education all-new-hire estimate is 0.022 (SE 0.012), marked with the table's marginal-significance symbol (p. 14, Table 3, panel A, row 1, SPED column).
- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution reviews: pre-adoption patterns are reassuring, retention estimates are broadly stable in spatial checks, and hiring-origin estimates move toward zero with wider exclusions; this is visual supporting evidence, not a formal proof of identification (pp. 13, 15, 17–18, Figures 2–5).
- CONFIRMED — Methods review: saturation is fixed at adoption (p. 19); the turnover interaction is 0.010 (SE 0.050), with reported saturation SD about 0.095, reproducing the review's approximate −0.84 to +1.03 percentage-point interval for that exposure difference (p. 20, Table 5, panel A and note).
- CONFIRMED — Writing/reproducibility reviews: Equation 1 uses '4DSW_{jt+1}' (p. 6), whereas Equation 4 uses '4DSW_{jt}' (p. 10); visual inspection confirms a printed discrepancy, with implementation unresolved.
- CONFIRMED — Writing review: Figure 3 says 'new teacher FTE shares' in its caption but 'Change in Teacher Retention' on its axis (p. 15); Figure 5 labels a panel 'Total FTEs' but its note specifies 'new-teacher FTE shares' (p. 18).
- CONFIRMED — Writing review: Table 6 says 'Teacher-level regressions' but labels its observations 'district-years' (p. 20), while the recruitment method explicitly describes 'aggregating our data to the district level' (p. 10).
- CONFIRMED — Literature review: the focal paper says rural turnover exceeds that in 'urban and suburban areas' (p. 2), but the cited source says 'overall rural public school teacher turnover is about average'; this is a background citation problem, not a refutation of the Missouri estimates ([Ingersoll and Tran, discussion of Table 3](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0013161X231159922)).
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reviews' accounts of supplemental robustness results cannot be verified against exhibits: online appendices are not bound into the supplied PDF; descriptions in the article are author-reported evidence (pp. 10–11, 19–23).
